takeaway: This curriculum is a 70-day, phase-structured build: each day layers one governance or architecture concept onto the last, so treat the daily recap/peek sections as the connective tissue that keeps the whole arc coherent.

SCPs are a permission ceiling, not a grant — they cap what an account can do but an IAM identity still needs its own allow, and the default FullAWSAccess SCP permits everything until you attach explicit Deny statements.
hooks: global services exemption (IAM, Route 53, CloudFront, Support)

takeaway: Control Tower automates the landing zone you'd otherwise build by hand — management, log-archive, and audit accounts plus guardrails implemented as SCPs and Config rules — and AFT extends that to pipeline-driven account provisioning.
IAM Identity Center replaces per-account IAM users with permission sets mapped to SAML federation from an external IdP, auto-provisioning an IAM role into each assigned account.

A permission boundary caps the maximum permissions an IAM entity can ever hold even when its attached policies are broader, and STS issues the short-lived credentials that make all this federation work.
AWS RAM lets a central network account share subnets, Transit Gateways, and Resolver rules with other accounts so app teams launch into a centrally owned VPC without owning it.
Week 1's pieces compose into one enterprise governance model: landing zone design, SCP guardrails, Control Tower automation, centralized SSO, and shared networking all reinforce each other.

Transit Gateway replaces an unmanageable full mesh of VPC peering with a regional hub-and-spoke, where each attachment associates with one TGW route table and propagates routes into others for fine-grained segmentation.
TGW peering runs across regions over the AWS backbone, but peering attachments do not propagate routes — you must add them statically — and inter-region MTU is capped at 1500 bytes.
hooks: no route propagation on peering attachments

takeaway: Network Firewall does stateful and stateless inspection with Suricata-compatible rules, typically in a centralized inspection VPC that all traffic is routed through via TGW and appliance-VPC route table tricks.

Direct Connect gives you a dedicated private link into AWS, with Private VIFs for one VPC, Transit VIFs for a TGW, and Public VIFs for public endpoints — and real resilience needs redundant connections and locations with BGP failover.

Route 53 Resolver bridges hybrid DNS: Inbound endpoints let on-prem resolvers query AWS private hosted zones, while Outbound endpoints plus forwarding rules let AWS resources resolve on-prem names over DX or VPN.

PrivateLink exposes a single service across accounts via an ENI-backed Interface Endpoint with no peering, no route table changes, and no CIDR conflicts — while Gateway endpoints (S3/DynamoDB only) use route table entries and are free.
hooks: exposing one microservice to many accounts

takeaway: Week 2 consolidates hybrid connectivity decision-making — TGW vs peering vs PrivateLink, DX resiliency patterns, and hybrid DNS — one of the highest-weight clusters on the exam.
Fargate runs ECS tasks with no EC2 to manage, each task getting its own isolated compute allocation from a task definition, and awsvpc networking gives every task its own ENI and security group.

EKS runs the Kubernetes control plane as a managed service, and you choose worker capacity from self-managed nodes, managed node groups, or Fargate profiles — with Fargate losing DaemonSets and costing more per pod.

Lifecycle hooks pause instances in Pending:Wait or Terminating:Wait so bootstrap and drain scripts can run, and warm pools keep pre-initialized stopped instances ready to scale out without full boot latency.
hooks: deregister from load balancer in hook

takeaway: ALB routes by path, host, header, or query string to multiple target groups, supports weighted target groups for blue/green and canary shifting, and can target Lambda directly.

Reserved concurrency caps and guarantees a function's max concurrency while provisioned concurrency pre-warms environments to kill cold starts, and event source mapping polls Kinesis, DynamoDB Streams, and SQS in batches with per-source concurrency and error handling.

Step Functions orchestrates multi-step workflows with built-in retry/catch and a Standard (exactly-once, auditable) vs Express (high-throughput, at-least-once) split, while API Gateway fronts them with REST/HTTP APIs and native integrations that bypass Lambda for simple pass-through.
hooks: API Gateway native service integrations bypassing Lambda

takeaway: Week 3 consolidates compute choice: ECS vs EKS, serverless vs server-based, Fargate vs managed nodes, and scaling mechanics — with scenario questions hinging on operational overhead, cost, and control.
hooks: operational overhead vs cost vs control

takeaway: Aurora decouples compute from a self-healing storage layer replicated 6 ways across 3 AZs, and Aurora Global Database adds cross-region replication via the storage layer (not binlog) with sub-second lag and sub-minute promotion.
hooks: secondary region promotable in under a minute

takeaway: Multi-AZ is for HA with a synchronous standby and same endpoint but does not scale reads, read replicas scale reads asynchronously with data-loss risk on promotion, and Blue/Green Deployments give a synchronized staging environment for safer upgrades.
hooks: async read replicas with promotion data-loss risk

takeaway: DynamoDB partitions by hash of the partition key, so low-cardinality or hot keys throttle regardless of table throughput, and on-demand vs provisioned capacity is a predictability-vs-cost trade-off.

DynamoDB Global Tables give you multi-region, multi-active writes with last-writer-wins conflict resolution, while DAX is an in-memory read-through/write-through cache that drops read latency from milliseconds to microseconds.

S3 storage classes trade cost against retrieval latency and availability, lifecycle rules automate the transitions and expirations, and CRR/SRR replicate objects asynchronously for DR or data residency.

Redis is the choice whenever HA, persistence, or complex data structures matter (with Global Datastore for cross-region), while Memcached is a simple, multi-threaded, non-persistent cache with no replication.

This synthesis locks in the database/storage selection matrix — relational vs key-value vs cache, consistency models, and the global replication trade-off between Aurora Global DB and DynamoDB Global Tables.
hooks: Aurora Global DB vs DynamoDB Global Tables
thread: PHASE-CLOSE: the data selection matrix thread

takeaway: CloudWatch alarms fire on static thresholds or ML-based anomaly detection bands, and composite alarms combine multiple alarm states with AND/OR logic so you only page on a true incident pattern like high latency AND high error rate together.
hooks: high latency AND high error rate

takeaway: Synthetics canaries are scripted Puppeteer/Selenium probes that exercise your endpoints and user flows from outside your infrastructure, catching availability and latency SLO breaches before real users report them.

X-Ray traces a request across microservices into a service map that highlights per-hop latency and error hotspots, with sampling rules controlling cost and annotations/subsegments letting you drill into a specific slow downstream call.

Logs Insights gives you a query language over CloudWatch Logs for ad-hoc analysis, while subscription filters stream logs in real time to a centralized logging account for org-wide search, retention, and SIEM ingestion.

FIS runs controlled chaos experiments — EC2/ECS/EKS termination, CPU/network stress, RDS/AZ failover — defined as experiment templates with mandatory stop conditions tied to CloudWatch alarms that halt the experiment if production stability is threatened.
hooks: stop conditions tied to CloudWatch alarms

takeaway: A Game Day is a scheduled exercise simulating a real failure — AZ outage, dependency failure, region loss — to validate that runbooks, alarms, and automated recovery actually work, turning DR assumptions into tested facts.

Active-active serves live traffic from two or more regions at once, requiring multi-region replication with conflict resolution and global traffic steering via Route 53 latency/geoproximity routing or Global Accelerator anycast IPs for network-layer failover.
DR strategies form a cost/RTO spectrum — Backup & Restore (hours-days), Pilot Light (~tens of minutes), Warm Standby (minutes), and Multi-Site Active-Active (lowest RTO/RPO, highest cost).

Route 53 ARC adds readiness checks that continuously validate a standby region can actually take over, plus routing controls on a control plane independent of any single region for deterministic, auditable failover.
hooks: control plane independent of a single region
safer than ad hoc health-check failover

takeaway: Route 53 routing policies — simple, weighted, latency, failover, geolocation, geoproximity with bias, and multi-value — each pair with health checks that automatically pull unhealthy endpoints out of DNS responses.

AWS Backup centralizes policy-based backup across EBS, RDS, DynamoDB, and EFS with schedules, lifecycle, and cross-region/cross-account copy, while Vault Lock enforces WORM immutability for compliance and ransomware protection.

The Reliability pillar rests on four areas — foundations (service quotas, network topology), workload architecture (distributed design, graceful degradation), change management, and failure management with tested recovery.

Operational Excellence means performing operations as code (IaC, automated runbooks), making frequent small reversible changes, anticipating failure via game days, and learning from blameless post-incident reviews.

This synthesis consolidates observability (metrics, tracing, synthetics), chaos engineering, and DR pattern selection from backup/restore through active-active — the SRE cluster central to the exam's resilience domain.

The 7 Rs classify each workload's move — Retire, Retain, Rehost (MGN), Relocate (VMware Cloud on AWS), Repurchase (SaaS), Replatform (lift-tinker-and-shift), Refactor — with Migration Hub tracking progress across tools.
hooks: Relocate to VMware Cloud on AWS

takeaway: Application Discovery Service (agent-based or agentless) inventories on-prem servers, dependencies, and utilization data to build a data-driven migration plan and right-size target instances, feeding into Migration Hub.

MGN performs continuous low-impact block-level replication from source servers to a staging area in AWS, letting you launch test and cutover instances at any point with minimal downtime — the standard rehost tool replacing CloudEndure/SMS.

SCT converts schema, views, stored procedures, and functions between different engines and reports a conversion-completeness percentage, but even 95% leaves complex procedural code needing manual remediation — SCT handles schema, DMS handles data.

DataSync automates and accelerates online transfer of files and objects between on-prem storage (NFS, SMB, HDFS) and AWS storage (S3, EFS, FSx) with scheduling, encryption, bandwidth throttling, and integrity validation — and unlike DMS it is not database-aware.

Storage Gateway comes in three distinct flavors — File (S3 as NFS/SMB share), Volume (iSCSI block backed by S3 in cached or stored mode), and Tape (virtual tape library replacing physical tape) — and picking the right one depends on whether the on-prem workload speaks file, block, or tape.
hooks: File Gateway NFS/SMB share backed by S3
Volume Gateway cached vs stored mode

takeaway: The Snow Family is the offline-transfer answer when the network is the bottleneck: Snowcone for small/rugged edge, Snowball Edge Storage Optimized (~80TB usable) or Compute Optimized with GPU, and Snowmobile for exabyte-scale shipping-container transfers.
hooks: Snowball Edge Compute Optimized with GPU

takeaway: Outposts, Local Zones, and Wavelength all push AWS infrastructure closer to the workload, but for different reasons — Outposts for data residency and on-prem latency, Local Zones for metro latency without owning hardware, Wavelength for 5G mobile edge.
hooks: Outposts extends AWS APIs into your data center
Local Zones in specific metro areas

takeaway: The Relocate strategy moves VMware workloads to VMware Cloud on AWS without converting them to native EC2/AMI, preserving the hypervisor and VMware tooling — often an interim step before a later native refactor.

Large-scale migrations need Direct Connect capacity (or LAG-bundled connections) provisioned ahead of the window, and the hybrid pattern of Snowball for the bulk historical dataset plus DX/DMS CDC for the ongoing delta is a common exam answer.
hooks: provision DX capacity ahead of migration window

takeaway: Match the commitment to the workload: Compute Savings Plans for maximum flexibility, EC2 Instance Savings Plans for cheaper but family/region-locked savings, RIs when you also need capacity reservation, and Spot (up to ~90% off) with Spot Fleet/mixed-instance ASGs for fault-tolerant work.
hooks: EC2 Instance Savings Plans locked to family/region

takeaway: Compute Optimizer turns utilization metrics into right-sizing recommendations, Cost Explorer visualizes and forecasts spend (and drives RI/Savings Plan purchase advice), and Trusted Advisor flags cost, security, performance, and fault-tolerance issues against best practices.
hooks: Cost Explorer forecasts and RI purchase recommendations

takeaway: FinOps on AWS starts with consistent tagging (enforced via SCPs/Config rules) so Cost Allocation Reports can attribute spend by team/project/environment, with AWS Budgets alerting on overspend and CUR providing the most granular billing data for custom tooling.
hooks: AWS Budgets forecasted vs actual alerts
Cost and Usage Report (CUR) granular billing data

takeaway: DMS is one of the highest-yield exam topics (3-4 questions typically): know full load vs CDC, replication instance sizing, LOB handling, and the DMS+SCT pattern for heterogeneous migrations.
hooks: AWS DMS full load vs CDC

takeaway: Sit a full 75-question, 180-minute timed mock under real conditions to establish a baseline score and internalize SAP-C02 pacing (~2.4 min/question average, with scenario questions needing more).

Distractor analysis is the real work: for every missed question — and every question you got right by luck or elimination — articulate why the correct answer is right and why each distractor is wrong, then tag each miss by domain to find your weakest area.
Targeted deep review of Weeks 1-2 (multi-account governance and hybrid networking) focused specifically on whatever Domain 1 weak areas Day 58's analysis flagged.
Targeted deep review of Weeks 3-6 (compute, databases, SRE/DR) focused on the Domain 2 weak areas flagged by mock exam analysis.
Second full timed mock exam — the point is comparing the score delta against Mock Exam 1 to see whether the Day 59-60 deep review actually closed the gaps it targeted.
hooks: did the deep review close the gaps

takeaway: Repeat the Day 58 distractor-analysis process for Mock Exam 2, tracking whether previously weak domains improved or whether new gaps emerged.
Deep review of Weeks 7-8 migration content — the 7 Rs, MGN, DMS/SCT, DataSync, Snow Family, hybrid networking capacity — focused on flagged Domain 3 weak areas.
Deep review of cost optimization content — Savings Plans vs RIs vs Spot, Compute Optimizer, FinOps tagging/budgets — focused on flagged Domain 4 weak areas.
hooks: Savings Plans vs RIs vs Spot

takeaway: Third full timed mock exam — by this point scores should be trending consistently toward the 80%+ target range.
Beyond content review, analyze time-per-question data from Mock Exam 3 to find which question types cost the most time, and refine the flag-and-skip strategy accordingly.
hooks: which question types cost the most time

takeaway: Fourth full timed mock exam, ideally from a different question bank/vendor than exams 1-3 to reduce pattern memorization and test genuine understanding.
Final full distractor-analysis pass, refining the flag-and-review technique: which questions do you consistently need a second look at, and why.
Fifth and final full timed mock exam — target consistently scoring above 85% before sitting the real exam.
Light review only the day before the exam: re-read your personal weak-spot cheat sheet, confirm Pearson VUE/OnVUE logistics (ID, room scan, check-in time), and resist cramming new material.
